title: An Unexplained State
logline: A rectangular shaft of clear water cut into a flat limestone plain was measured by a writer whose own journal could not find his name: he let a valved bottle down to the salt water and to the floor, levelled the country from coast to coast, sat by the water from six in the morning to six at night, and then wrote that the one thing he had come to explain 'remains in an unexplained state'. The camera goes down his line as far as the fresh water goes, stops where the salt begins, and looks back up.
human_question: When I measure something and part of it still will not come clear, is what I am left with a fault in me, or just the honest size of what I know?

place.what_kind_of_place: A natural shaft in the limestone of a very flat, very dry coastal peninsula: a rectangular pit about twelve metres by eight, open to the sky, with the water standing some four metres below the ground and going down, in clear fresh water over heavier salt water, to a floor more than forty metres below. The rim has been lined with rendered masonry, stepped down to the water and fenced; around it is open red-soil cultivation, palmyra and scrub, and a horizon with nothing on it. Above ground it is a small and plain place. Below the surface it is a vertical room of pale rock and falling light, and at some depth between about twelve and eighteen metres the fresh water ends on a layer of salt.
place.why_it_is_worth_watching: Not for the rim. The film is worth making for what the water does with noon light. A shaft this narrow and this clear turns a high sun into columns that run straight down the walls into blue and then into dark; a diver's camera hanging on a line inside them sees rock, light and depth and nothing else. Where fresh water sits on salt the two do not mix at once, and the boundary bends light: the view through it wavers like air over a hot road, a floor of shimmer with the darker water under it. And from inside the shaft, looking up, the surface is a bright rectangle of sky set in black rock, the same cut in the ground the film began above, seen from the underside. Three shots: the columns, the boundary, the window. None of them can be had anywhere on land.
place.what_moves_or_changes: The light, which is the only thing the film waits for: it reaches deepest when the sun is highest, and at this latitude the sun stands directly overhead twice a year. The water level, by fractions of an inch, which a nineteenth-century observer recorded rising and falling three times between dawn and dusk on the day he watched. The line: a weighted line lowered by the crew, down which the camera travels, standing in for the sounding line and the valved bottle of the old account. Nothing else in the film moves on purpose.
place.when_it_looks_best: Solar noon on a clear, still day in the dry months, and best of all within a few days of the two dates when the noon sun passes directly overhead at this latitude (around mid-April and the end of August, computed from the latitude and not observed). After heavy rain or pumping, or with wind on the surface, the columns break up and the shoot should wait.

two_layers.without_the_philosophy: A descent film. Heat and flatness above: a plain with nothing on it, a cut in the ground, steps down to a square of turquoise. Then under: a camera sinking on a line through columns of noon light in a shaft of pale rock, the blue deepening, until the water ahead goes glassy and wavering where fresh gives way to salt. The camera stops there, hangs, and tilts up to the bright rectangle of sky far overhead. A beginning in heat, a middle in falling light, and a payoff looking back the way it came. There is no drone and no music, and no one is on screen except, at most, the edge of a diver's hand on the line.
two_layers.with_the_philosophy: The same descent follows a document. A paper of the 1860s, printed without its author's name, set out to measure the well's depth, its salt water and its small tides, and said at the start that it would offer no theory. It measured the depth and the salt, and on the tides it said the question was still open. The voice lays that record beside the two texts' account of doubt. Both texts count doubt as one of the fourteen unwholesome factors, and both say that ordinary not-knowing about something one does not know is not it: the doubt they count is a mind that cannot settle, like a traveller worn out at a fork, and its object is the teacher and the teaching. The film never says what anyone's mind was doing. It shows what an examination settled, what it left open, and what was said about the open part. The texts say that examining an object well is what dispels doubt. What was left here after the measuring is the kind of not-knowing they do not count.

sequence.on_screen: Solar noon. A locked wide frame at eye height: a flat plain of red soil and pale stone running to a horizon with nothing on it, palmyra standing in the heat, and in the middle distance a low fenced rim around a cut in the ground. Wind, no other sound. Held long.
sequence.voice: The old books on the mind list fourteen things that make a moment of mind unwholesome. The last of them is doubt. They describe it with a picture: a traveller comes for the first time to a place where the road divides, cannot settle which way to go, and wears himself out standing there. They count that kind of doubt as heavy as a wrong view.

sequence.on_screen: At the rim, then down the steps: rendered masonry stepping four metres to the water, and the water itself from directly above the edge, clear enough that the rock wall is visible going down into blue. A weighted line is paid out into the middle of it and runs out of sight.
sequence.voice: This water was called bottomless, and in the 1860s someone decided to find out. The paper he wrote was printed in the island's learned journal, and the journal's editor added a footnote saying he had been unable to find out the author's name. The paper begins by saying it will not try to explain anything, or offer any theory. It will simply narrate facts and leave the cause to others.

sequence.on_screen: Under the surface. The camera, hanging on the line, sinks slowly through columns of noon light that run straight down the pale walls. Natural light only. No cut.
sequence.voice: He wrote down what was said about the well before he tested it: a tradition that joined it under the ground to springs on the coast. He did not call the tradition false. He wrote that it was only tradition, because no one could trace the course of a spring through country this flat. That is one kind of not knowing. The shorter of the two texts names it directly: about things they do not know, everyone wonders whether it is this way or that way, and that is not the doubt meant here.

sequence.on_screen: Deeper on the line. The blue thickens and the walls go darker; the columns of light narrow as they fall. The camera keeps sinking, slowly, at an even rate.
sequence.voice: Then he measured. He took levels right across the country from one coast to the other, and found the surface of this fresh water standing almost exactly at the sea's low-water mark on both sides. He let down a bottle with a valve that could be opened and shut at any depth. The water turned brackish somewhere between forty and fifty feet. The bottle touched the floor at about a hundred and forty-five, and what it brought up from there smelt strongly of sulphur. The well was not bottomless. The texts say that doubt goes when the mind examines its object well, and on this question the measuring did exactly that.

sequence.on_screen: The camera slows and stops above the boundary. Ahead and below, the clear water turns glassy and wavering where fresh sits on salt; the rock and the line seen through it bend and shimmer. The camera hangs there, still, for a long time. The voice is silent for the first part of the hold.
sequence.voice: On the tides the result was different. The water in this well rises and falls, by fractions of an inch. He and a medical officer watched it every half hour from six in the morning to six at night while assistants watched the sea on both coasts. The well turned three times in the day, and at one point it rose while the sea fell. He wrote that this alone destroyed every explanation he had heard, and that the subject 'remains in an unexplained state'. A later survey by divers put the floor deeper than he did and the fresh water deeper too. The two sets of figures do not agree, and neither is wrong just because the other exists.

sequence.on_screen: Still at the boundary. The camera turns slowly from the shimmer below to the rock wall beside it, close enough to see its grain in the last of the light, and holds.
sequence.voice: The texts are exact about where the doubt they count can occur. Of the twelve kinds of unwholesome mind, only one has it: a mind rooted in delusion, which they picture as a darkness over the object. The older text is careful about the rest. Not being able to settle a matter one does not know, it says, may not be unwholesome at all. A camera cannot see which of these is present in anyone, and this film does not try. What it can show is a record that stops where its evidence stops and says so.

sequence.on_screen: The payoff. The camera tilts up from the boundary, all the way. Far overhead, the surface: a bright rectangle of sky set in black rock, the cut in the ground from the first shot, seen from underneath, with the line running up into it. Held until the frame is nearly still, then cut to black.
sequence.voice: The texts do not ask anyone to be certain. They ask not to be stuck at the fork. His paper ends by calling the unexplained part 'a field for scientific enquiry and discussion'. That is not a traveller who cannot choose a road. It is a record of how far the road has been walked.

concept_merge.why_together: C022 supplies the factor and its boundary. Doubt is the last of the fourteen unwholesome factors [C022-P:L31; C022-M:L3]: a mind unable to settle its object, like a traveller at a fork, a hindrance as strong as wrong view [C022-P:L179]. Both sources then fence it off from ordinary not-knowing: Margaya says flatly that everyone wonders 'is it so or so?' about things they do not know and that this is not the factor, the unwholesome kind being doubt about the teacher and the teaching [C022-M:L57]; Pradeepika says a doubt that is not a hindrance, arising from not being able to settle something one does not know, 'may possibly not be unwholesome' [C022-P:L179], and that examining the object well dispels doubt [C022-P:L183]. C026 supplies where it can occur: in one of the twelve unwholesome minds only, the delusion-rooted mind accompanied by doubt, and in none of the other eighty-eight [C026-P:L51; C026-P:L61; C026-M:L9], a mind that always carries the four common factors with delusion first [C026-P:L29; C026-M:L3].
concept_merge.what_it_reveals: Together they make the exempt case precise enough to film without accusing anyone. C022 alone would tempt the film to call the unexplained tides 'doubt' and the old belief 'wrong'; C026 alone would be a counting scheme. Joined, they say the doubt the texts count lives in one specific mind, rooted in delusion, and concerns the teacher and the teaching; ordinary not-knowing about a spring, a floor or a tide is outside it, and examination is what moves a question from one side of the line to the other. The well's record shows both halves in sequence: a question examination settled (the floor) and a question it narrowed but left open (the tides), with the open part written down as open. The test finding in the brief, that the ordinary-uncertainty exemption applies here, was checked against the lines themselves: it is firm in Margaya and hedged in Pradeepika ('may possibly not be'), and the film keeps the hedge.

concept_links.why: The film is built on the one place both C022 sources draw a line through their own factor. Doubt is listed last of the fourteen [C022-P:L31; C022-M:L3] and defined as the inability to settle an object, a hindrance as strong as wrong view, pictured as a traveller wearied at a fork he reaches for the first time [C022-P:L179]. Then both exempt the ordinary case: Margaya says wondering 'is it so or so?' about things one does not know is not this factor, and names the unwholesome doubt as doubt about the teacher and the teaching [C022-M:L57]; Pradeepika says the doubt of not being able to settle an unknown matter is not a hindrance and 'may possibly not be unwholesome', and adds that developing the examining of an object well dispels doubt [C022-P:L179; C022-P:L183]. The ruling this record makes, after reading both lines: the film's case is exempt under Margaya without qualification and probably exempt under Pradeepika, whose wording is a possibility rather than a verdict, and the voice says so rather than smoothing the two into one. The document carries it: a paper that records a tradition as untraceable rather than false, settles the floor by measurement, and leaves the tides expressly unexplained. Three does_not_transfer lines bind the film. 'Questioning is a vice' is forbidden, and the film is built to show the opposite. Nothing is said about the unwholesome doubt's real object, doubt about the teacher and the teaching, beyond naming it, and no belief of any living tradition is set up as the thing doubted or dispelled. And the digest's note that its eight objects of doubt are not listed in the extract [C022-P:L179] means the film does not list them either.

C026 gives the film its limit and its sixth beat. Doubt occurs, fixed, in only one of the twelve unwholesome minds, the delusion-rooted mind accompanied by doubt, and in none of the other eighty-eight [C026-P:L51; C026-P:L55–L61; C026-M:L9]; that mind, like every unwholesome mind, carries the delusion tetrad [C026-P:L29; C026-M:L3], delusion being what hides an object's real nature [C022-P:L35; C022-M:L7]. The fourteen factors occur only in the twelve unwholesome minds and never in the other seventy-seven [C026-P:L25], which is why the exemption matters: ordinary not-knowing does not have to be squeezed into that one mind. The digest's first does_not_transfer line is written into the voice almost word for word: this is a study scheme about single moments, not a diagnostic tool, and a camera cannot show which factor is present. The film therefore never says what the paper's author, the diving party or any visitor was thinking; the author is anonymous, which removes any temptation to make him an exhibit, and the voice describes only what his record does.

what_the_viewer_could_understand: That the texts' doubt is a narrow, specific thing and not a name for every open question; that an honest record can settle one part of a question, leave another open, and say which is which; and that 'I do not know yet', written down with the measurements beside it, is on the texts' own account a different thing from the mind that stands at a fork and cannot go on.
what_must_be_real: The shaft, the clear water, the columns of noon light and the fresh-over-salt boundary, filmed as found with natural light and no added lamps, dye or particles. The line in frame is the crew's own and is described as such in production notes; it is not presented as the 1860s instrument. Every figure in the voice is the 1860s paper's own or the later survey's own, kept separate. No reconstruction of the nineteenth-century measuring party, no actors, no animation of tides.
position_hint: Late in the group, after the films on anger, envy and stinginess and before or beside the group's other doubt film: this one is the group's only natural landform and its only film below the surface, and it lets the group's run of aversion end on a question that examination has partly answered rather than on a verdict.
risks: Calling the unexplained tides 'doubt' in the texts' sense, or calling the old tradition 'wrong view'. Both are forbidden by the digests' exemption and by the does_not_transfer line against making questioning a vice; the voice keeps the tradition as the paper kept it, untraceable rather than false.

Drifting into the unwholesome doubt's real object. The texts place it on the teacher and the teaching; the film names that once and goes no further, and nothing on screen stands for a religious doubt.

A living religious story. A widely repeated modern tradition says the well was made by an arrow shot by Rama. It is a living Hindu tradition, its earliest attestation was not reached, and the 1860s paper does not mention it (silence, not denial). It is neither narrated nor corrected; it is kept out of the film entirely.

Archaeology and territory. A limestone Buddha torso and the remains of a stupa have been reported near the well, and some web pages say the divers found the torso in the water. Buddhist archaeology in this district touches live territorial and religious claims. None of it enters the film, the frame or the voice.

War. The district's recent history is out of bounds as subject. The later survey is described in the voice only as a survey by divers, not by the service that carried it out, and nothing in the film touches the war.

Death. A body is reported to have been recovered from this well by navy divers (a video title, not verified), and the later survey is reported to have found remains on the floor. The camera never goes below the boundary, never films the floor, and nothing in the film refers to loss of life. If a recent death is associated with the site at the time of shooting, the shoot is abandoned (see drop_if).

Collision with the peninsula's other water film (IDEA-0120), a coastal freshwater spring and bathing tank opened on a first-light overhead drone shot of a still rectangle of water. This film has no drone and no overhead frame of the surface, spends its length below the surface, and never refers to that spring. The popular claim that the two are joined underground is not used.

Water supply. Earlier pumping for irrigation and reported modern pumping put this near the used-up hydro and water-supply archetype. The 1824 pumping trial appears only as the evidence that the level could not be moved; any pump works at the rim stay out of frame, and the film says nothing about irrigation.

Diver safety. The shaft reaches roughly 43 to 52 m, has reported side passages, and the 1860s bottom sample smelt of hydrogen sulphide. The shoot is limited to the fresh layer and the boundary, roughly 12 to 18 m in an open shaft, on a fixed line, with no entry into any passage and no descent into the salt layer.
Visitors. People swim here from a platform. No swimmer or visitor is filmed as a subject; the underwater work is done when the water is empty.

A second exempt-doubt film in the same group (IDEA-0045, proposed). This one is about a natural fact measured and left partly open by one anonymous record; that one is about a carved figure whose identity named scholars keep deciding and re-deciding. The payoffs differ (a view up through the water against a sharp but unreadable object), and this film does not use the 'teacher or king?' question.
drop_if: Underwater visibility at the shoot is too poor for the light columns and the boundary to be seen; the rim alone does not carry the film.
Permission for a camera dive in the shaft is refused by the site's authorities, or a safe dive to the boundary cannot be planned without entering passages or the salt layer.
The fresh-over-salt boundary is not visible as a shimmer at the depths reported, or lies below the safe limit set for the shoot.
A recent death or a live dispute (religious, archaeological or territorial) attaches to the site at the time of shooting.
The rim and steps cannot be filmed without pump works, crowds or swimmers dominating every frame.

connections.note: The same limestone country's other water film: a coastal spring rising into a walled bathing tank, opened on a first-light overhead drone shot of a still rectangle of water and held on the surface all day, about matter as a continuous stream. This film is inland, at noon, has no drone and no overhead surface shot, and spends its length below the surface on a written record. It never refers to the spring, and it does not use the popular claim that the two waters are joined underground.

The district's other GRP-01-era neighbour: a five-sided colonial fort on a lagoon, an afternoon-to-dusk film of edges and the materials in a wall. Same district, nothing else shared: that is geometry and masonry in raking light, this is a natural shaft filmed from inside at noon. Neither film touches the war.

Proposed for the same group: a rock-cut figure of disputed identity filmed at dawn in fog, tripod, rack focus, no drone, on the difference between exempt scholarly uncertainty and the doubt that cannot decide. Both rest on the same exemption. That film is about a meaning that named scholars keep deciding and re-deciding; this one is about a physical fact that one anonymous record partly settled by measurement and partly left open, and says which part is which. Fog on land against clear water from inside; a held rack focus against a vertical descent.

The group's other film built on a document: a colossal inscribed slab whose sentence urges the removal of a man for a thought, filmed in a level traverse at page height. That text asks for action on a suspicion; this one declines to offer even a theory beyond its evidence.

selection.reason: Carries C022's exempt case, the only honest way a camera can approach doubt, on a primary document that turns on it: an anonymous 1865-66 paper that declines to theorise, records a tradition as untraceable rather than false, settles the depth by measurement and leaves the well's small tides expressly unexplained. The document was reached and read in the journal itself, which corrected several popular facts, including the author's name. The location was a blind colleague's proposal and was tested: the story passes strongly; the footage half passes only below the surface, and the record says so and gives the conditions for dropping it.

review.note: The body of this record was replaced entirely on 2026-09-26 in the blind GRP-03 rework and rebuilt from fresh research; the previous body was not read. The old status was pending, so no confirmation or rejection has been reset, but under standing decision 9 any earlier reading of this record no longer applies. The concepts are unchanged (C022 primary, C026 supporting). The title is new; the old title is kept in aliases. The location, named in suggested_location, is a natural limestone shaft of fresh water over salt water on a flat northern peninsula; it takes its district from 3 to 4 films. It was a blind colleague's proposal and was tested rather than assumed. The primary source was reached: the paper on the well in the 1865-66 number of the Royal Asiatic Society branch journal (vol. 4, printed 1866), read in two archive.org scans. It corrected the proposal and its web sources in several places: the author is not 'Folkart' (the journal's own footnote says the editor could not find the author's name); the depth given is 140 to 145 ft, about 42.7 to 44.2 m, not 45 to 46 m; brackish water began 'between 40 and 50 ft', about 12 to 15 m; the 'three tides a day' were three alternations seen on one day between 6 a.m. and 6 p.m., of fractions of an inch; the tradition the paper records links the well to springs at a named point on the coast, not to the spring filmed in IDEA-0120, and calls it untraceable rather than false; and the paper reports an 1824 pumping trial that could not move the level. The proposal's treatment was changed: its opening top-down drone shot of the dark rectangle would have repeated IDEA-0120's opening at another limestone water body in the same peninsula, so this film has no drone and no overhead surface frame, and its payoff is the view up from the fresh-salt boundary, not the boundary itself (the proposed IDEA-0045 already pays off on something seen sharp but unreadable). The strongest objection is that above water this is a small, rendered and fenced pit, and the film lives or dies on a camera dive: if visibility, permission or a safe plan to reach the boundary fails, it should be dropped, not weakened. Second objection: it is a second limestone-water film in one district; the answer is a different story shape, concept, time of day and camera position, but a reviewer may reasonably count it as a neighbour too close. The Rama legend, the Buddha torso and ruins nearby, the war, and a reported recovery of a body from the well are all kept out of the film. Still unverified: visibility, the depth of the boundary today, dive permission, current pumping at the rim, and the date of the later naval survey.

suggested_location.name: Nilavarai well (the 'bottomless well'; the 'Tidal Well of Poottoor' of the 1860s), Puttur / Navatkiri

also_known_as.name: Nilavarai
also_known_as.meaning: the local name of the well; its meaning was not established in this research

also_known_as.name: Tidal Well of Poottoor
also_known_as.meaning: the name the 1865-66 paper says the well had earned from its rise and fall

also_known_as.name: Nilavarai Bottomless Well
also_known_as.meaning: the tourist name, from the belief that it had no floor

suggested_location.region: Jaffna District, Northern Province: Valikamam East, in the village area of Navatkiri near Puttur, on the flat limestone plain of the Jaffna peninsula about 12 km north-east of Jaffna town in a straight line (computed from the coordinates). District confirmed by a Nominatim reverse geocode (Jaffna District) and by the OSM feature 'Nilavarai (Bottomless well), Puttur, Jaffna District'.
suggested_location.why_here: It is the one place found where a primary document asks the concept's exempt question in its own words. In 1865-66 an anonymous paper set out to test a well that local report called bottomless and tidal. It announced that it would offer no theory, recorded the local tradition as untraceable rather than false, levelled the peninsula from coast to coast, sampled the water at four depths with a valved bottle, found the floor at 140 to 145 feet, watched the level every half hour for twelve hours, and concluded that the well's rise and fall 'remains in an unexplained state and offers a field for scientific enquiry and discussion'. That is the distinction both C022 sources draw: ordinary not-knowing about an unknown matter, which examination can narrow, against the doubt that cannot settle and concerns the teacher and the teaching. The footage half is the shaft itself: clear water, noon light falling forty metres, and a visible boundary where fresh water lies on salt.

historical_thread.story: The well is a natural rectangular pit in the limestone of the Jaffna peninsula. The earliest account reached in this research is a paper headed 'Poottoor Well' in the Journal of the Ceylon Branch of the Royal Asiatic Society for 1865-6 (vol. 4, printed by F. Fonseka, Colombo, 1866), listed in the contents without an author and footnoted by the editor: 'I have been unable to find out the name of the author of this paper.' The paper opens by saying it 'will contain no attempts to explain these phenomena, or to suggest any theory as a basis for discussion. Simply narrating facts, I leave it for others to determine the cause.' It describes the peninsula as nearly flat, with fresh water in fissures of the limestone a few feet down and wells that turn brackish below a certain depth, and the well as 'a large rectangular pit in the limestone rock' about 40 feet by 25, with a slope cut down to the water. 'Tradition connects it with some springs on the Coast near Tondamanaar, but it is only tradition as it would be simply impossible to trace the course or source of any springs in so level a country.' The only earlier experiments, it says, were in 1824, 'when engines of considerable power were employed, to raise water from the well, with a view of irrigating the district', and established only that the level could not be affected nor its rise and fall checked, which had earned it the name 'the Tidal Well of Poottoor'. The paper names three peculiarities, the tide, salt water from between 45 and 50 feet to the bottom, and apparent inexhaustibility, and treats the 1824 trial as settling the third. Its experiments: a levelled section 17 miles from the south coast at Jaffna to Valvettithurai ('Yalvettytorre') on the north showed the well's fresh-water surface 'coincides almost exactly with the low water level of the sea on both coasts'; a valved instrument took samples at the surface, 45, 95 and 145 feet '(the bottom)', sealed and sent to England for analysis; brackishness began 'between 40 and 50 ft. down'; the bottom water 'smelt strongly of sulphureted hydrogen'; the fresh-water surface lay 14 feet below the ground and the total depth 'varies between 140 and 145 feet'. With 'Dr. Ferguson of the Army Medical Staff', the author watched the well while two assistants watched the Jaffna lagoon and the sea at Valvettithurai, every half hour from 6 a.m. to 6 p.m., and tabulated the rise and fall in inches. His conclusion: 'the well alternated 3 times during the day, whilst the sea was not affected to a similar extent. The well also rose whilst the sea fell, and this part alone destroys all hypotheses that I have as yet heard discussed. The subject therefore remains in an unexplained state and offers a field for scientific enquiry and discussion.' In the twenty-first century a Sri Lanka Navy team of divers with a remotely operated camera is reported to have found the floor at 52.5 m, fresh water to about 18.3 m and salt below, several passages leading off at different levels, and the wreckage of carts on the floor.
historical_thread.how_it_binds: C022's doubt is a mind that cannot settle its object, a traveller worn out at a fork; both sources then say that ordinary not-knowing about a matter one does not know is not this factor, and one says examining the object well dispels doubt. The 1860s paper is a written example of that boundary, made without any reference to it: it declines to theorise, keeps a tradition as tradition without calling it false, settles the depth by measurement, and marks the tides as open. The film does not need to read a mind into anyone to show the difference, because the difference is in the record's own sentences. C026 then limits the claim: the doubt the texts count sits in one delusion-rooted mind out of twelve, and a camera cannot see which factor is present, so the film describes what the record does and nothing about what its author felt.
what_is_certain: The paper 'Poottoor Well' is printed in the Journal of the Ceylon Branch of the Royal Asiatic Society for 1865-6 (vol. 4, printed 1866), pp. 123-127 in the scan read, between Gogerly's 'First Discourse' and Boake's 'Air Breathing Fish', and the contents list it without an author. Read in two archive.org scans (in.ernet.dli.2015.104373 and journalofceylonb45roya).
The same page carries the editor's footnote: 'I have been unable to find out the name of the author of this paper.' Both scans have it.
The paper states at the outset that it will offer no explanation or theory and will simply narrate facts.

The paper records a tradition connecting the well with springs on the coast near Tondamanaar and calls it 'only tradition' because such a course could not be traced in so level a country. It does not call it false.

The paper reports that in 1824 engines were used to raise water from the well for irrigation, and that the level could not be affected nor its rise and fall checked. This is attested here only; no earlier source was reached.

Dimensions given: about 40 ft by 25 ft; fresh-water surface 14 ft below ground; total depth 'between 140 and 145 feet' (about 42.7 to 44.2 m) in the reprint scan, with samples at 45, 95 and 145 ft '(the bottom)'.
Brackishness was first found 'between 40 and 50 ft. down' (about 12.2 to 15.2 m); the paper's list of peculiarities gives salt water 'from a depth of between 45 and 50 feet to the bottom'.
The bottom water 'smelt strongly of sulphureted hydrogen'.
Levels taken across 17 miles from the south to the north coast showed the well's surface almost exactly at low-water level on both coasts.

Observations every half hour from 6 a.m. to 6 p.m. at the well, the lagoon and the northern sea: the well 'alternated 3 times during the day', 'rose whilst the sea fell', and the author concluded the subject 'remains in an unexplained state'. The well's tabulated movements are fractions of an inch; the sea stations moved by up to a few inches.
The well is in Jaffna District (Nominatim reverse geocode; OSM feature at 9.75434, 80.0883).

C022: both sources exclude ordinary uncertainty about unknown matters from the unwholesome doubt [C022-P:L179; C022-M:L57]; Pradeepika adds that examining the object well dispels doubt [C022-P:L183]. C026: doubt occurs only in the one doubt-accompanied mind [C026-P:L51; C026-M:L9].
what_is_disputed: Author. Travel and cave sites (showcaves.com) name the author as 'Folkart'. The journal's own editor wrote that he could not find the author's name, and neither scan names one. 'Folkart' is unsourced and is not used.

Depth. The 1860s paper: 140 to 145 ft (one scan's OCR reads 148 in the sentence on total depth; the sample depth is 145 ft in both). A later naval survey as reported: 52.5 m (about 172 ft). Showcaves converts the old figure to '45 m to 46 m', which the paper does not support. A travel page gives '20-25 meters'. The figures are held apart and not averaged; the difference may reflect method, silt, the point sounded or error, and was not resolved.
Fresh water. The 1860s paper: brackish from between 40 and 50 ft. The later survey as reported: fresh to 18.3 m (60 ft). Some pages say 14-15 m. Not reconciled.

'Three tides a day, unlike the twice-daily sea' (showcaves and the blind proposal). The paper records three alternations on one day of observation between 6 a.m. and 6 p.m., not a daily pattern, and does not state the sea's cycle in that sentence; it says the sea was not affected to a similar extent and that the well rose while the sea fell.

The underground link. The 1860s tradition joins the well to springs near Tondamanaar on the coast. Modern pages say a lime (or lemon) thrown in reappears at Keerimalai; the earliest attestation of that version was not reached. Neither is narrated.

The Rama legend. Modern pages say Rama made the well with an arrow (variants give Hanuman, or Sita's thirst, or his army's). Earliest attestation not reached; the 1860s paper does not mention it (silence, not denial). A living Hindu tradition; not narrated as fact or as error.

The Buddha torso. One account (lankapradeepa, citing the Jaffna archaeological museum) says a cultivator found a limestone torso about 250 yards west of the well, entered in the museum on 9 December 1952; other pages say the naval divers found it in the well. The two cannot both be the same event as told. Kept out of the film entirely.
The later naval survey's date and publication were not found; pages say only 'recent' or 'about 150 years' after the 1860s paper.
Current pumping for irrigation at the well is reported by one page and was not verified.

what_to_film: One locked wide frame of the plain at solar noon from eye height: flatness, palmyra, the low fenced rim in the middle distance. No drone.

The rim and the steps down to the water, handheld at walking pace, and the water from directly above its edge, clear enough to show the wall going down into blue. Framed to exclude pump works, pipes and signage.
A weighted line lowered into the centre of the shaft by the crew, filmed from above as it runs out of sight.

The descent: one continuous diver-carried take on the fixed line, wide rectilinear lens, natural light only, from the surface through the columns of noon light to a stop just above the fresh-salt boundary. No lamps.
The boundary itself as seen from above it: the wavering, glassy layer where fresh water sits on salt, with the line and the wall bending through it. Held long.
The rock wall beside the camera at the boundary depth, close, for grain and the last of the light.
The payoff: a slow tilt from the boundary up to the surface, the lit rectangle of sky in dark rock, with the line running up into it. Held until nearly still.
Wild sound at the rim (wind, palmyra, heat) and the ambience of the shaft underwater, recorded separately; no score.
suggested_location.access: Open public site by road from Jaffna town, reported free to visit and without fixed restrictions (showcaves), with parking and a few stalls (nashaplaneta). People swim from a platform. The site is described by one source as an archaeological monument; permission for a camera dive would need to be sought from the Department of Archaeology and the local authority (Valikamam East), and a qualified dive team with surface support, a written dive plan limited to the fresh layer and the boundary, and no entry into side passages. Drone work is not part of this film. None of this has been checked with anyone.
suggested_location.best_time: Solar noon on a clear, windless day in the dry season. Best within a few days of the two dates when the noon sun is directly overhead at latitude 9.75 N, around mid-April and the end of August (computed, not observed). Avoid the north-east monsoon months, when the 1860s paper notes the peninsula's wells rise and when rain and runoff are likely to cloud the water; avoid days after heavy pumping. Underwater work early in the week or at hours when no one is swimming.

suggested_location.research_note: Desk research only; nothing on the ground, underwater or with any authority has been checked. DISTRICT: Jaffna moves from 3 to 4 films (IDEA-0009 Jaffna Fort, IDEA-0120 Keerimalai, IDEA-0176 Kaithady, and this); no GRP-02 pick and no other GRP-03 pick is in Jaffna, so it stays within the preferred band. PRIMARY SOURCE: the paper was read in full in two archive.org scans of JCBRAS vol. 4; quotations are from the scans' OCR, checked against each other where they differ (the reprint scan reads 'between 140 and 145 feet', the other '140 and 148'; both give the bottom sample at 145 ft). The tide table's individual figures are too damaged in both OCRs to quote; the record claims only what the author's own conclusion says and that the well's entries are fractions of an inch. No earlier account was found: Casie Chitty's Ceylon Gazetteer (1834) has an entry for Puttoor that does not mention the well, and Tennent's Ceylon (1859-60, both volumes) was searched without a hit; both are silences, not denials. The 1824 pumping trial is known only from the 1866 paper. FAILURE MODES TESTED: (1) chronicle not containing its story: no chronicle is used; (2) founding legend carried only by late texts: the Rama arrow story and the lime-to-Keerimalai story are attested in this research only on modern web pages, while the 1866 paper records a different, non-religious tradition (springs near Tondamanaar); neither legend is narrated; (3) figure repeated without source: '45-46 m', 'bottomless', '20-25 m' and 'Folkart' all corrected or set aside against the paper; (4) claim belonging to a different site or event: the Buddha torso found by a cultivator 250 yards away in or before 1952 is retold as a find of the divers; kept out; (5) impossible date: none found, but the naval survey is undated; (6) silence as denial: the 1866 paper's silence on Rama, and the 1834 gazetteer's silence on the well, are recorded as silences; (7) 'scholars attribute': no unnamed scholarship is relied on; (8) passage told halfway: the paper's tradition sentence is taken whole, including its refusal to call the tradition false, and its conclusion is taken whole, including the rise-while-the-sea-fell observation. WHO WROTE IT DOWN AND WHAT DID HE STAND TO GAIN: an unnamed writer, apparently a colonial official or engineer working with an army medical officer, whose paper explicitly declines to argue for any theory; the journal could not name him. The 1824 trial was an irrigation effort, which is why it tested only the level. ARCHETYPE: a natural karst shaft measured by a document; the slate's nearest neighbour is IDEA-0120, a coastal spring-fed bathing tank in the same limestone, which is a real neighbour in kind; the difference is argued in risks and connections, and a reviewer may still judge the pair too close. Underwater work elsewhere on the slate (IDEA-0004's sea-floor temple stones, IDEA-0186's reef) is marine and horizontal; this is fresh water and vertical. IMAGES: Commons holds one photograph of the well (confirmed by imageinfo); the second image is the surrounding plain, captioned as not the site. Nothing underwater exists on Commons. FALLBACK in a different district: the blind proposal named the Malwana 'Convention' of 1597 in Gampaha (a treaty whose authenticity historians dispute); it was not tested here and is visually weaker. WEAKEST POINTS: the above-water site is small, rendered and fenced; the film depends on water clarity, a permitted dive and a visible boundary at a safe depth, none verified.

unknowns: Underwater visibility on any given day, and whether the light columns reach the boundary depth.
The present depth of the fresh-salt boundary and whether it is visible as a shimmer; the two surveys differ.
Whether a camera dive is permitted, by whom, and on what conditions.
Whether pump works, pipes or signage at the rim can be kept out of frame, and whether pumping clouds the water.
The date, method and publication of the later naval survey.
The identity of the 1865-66 paper's author, which the journal itself could not supply.
Whether the site is formally protected as an archaeological monument, as one page says.
evidence_class_note: Editorial proposal. The location was proposed by Claude on 2026-09-26 and awaits Chathura's review; no verdict has been given. The historical thread rests on the anonymous 1865-66 learned-society paper, read in two scans; the later survey figures, the legends and the archaeological reports are secondary web sources and are marked as such. The digest citations are to source teaching; the application of the exemption to this record is editorial interpretation.
